candidates.source_summary: The council has struck a deal to acquire Middleton’s Warwick Mill.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has struck a deal to acquire Middleton’s Warwick Mill, in a huge boost to the ongoing regeneration of the area. Built in 1907, the Grade II listed structure stopped operating as a cotton mill in 1965 and has been vacant for at least a decade. In recent years, alongside its neighbour, 1960’s office building, London House, which the council is also hoping to acquire under the terms of the deal, the site has become an eyesore and a target for vandalism. For the past decade the council has been working with the private sector to find a solution for the imposing structure but none of the plans came to fruition and its condition has been gradually deteriorating. The council has been looking at buying the mill for a period of time, but a recent engagement exercise with local residents and businesses galvanised their decision. The exercise, titled ‘Our Town, Our Future’ saw local community organisation, Middleton Co-operating, engage with more than 2,000 residents to find out what they wanted for the area as part of wider work to create a Mayoral Development Corporation (MDC) for the area, which will be chaired by Middleton-born actor and comedian, Steve Coogan, and Rose Marley, chief executive of Co-operatives UK. Around a third of respondents said they would like to see Warwick Mill brought back into use. A number of people responding to the survey said that the building has huge potential and should be sensitively restored and brought back into use for the benefit of the wider community. candidates.source_body_excerpt: Plans for a football and community sports hub on playing fields in Middleton need to show the benefits outweigh any loss of current use, according to the body responsible for developing grass-roots sport. Sport England, which is a statutory consultee on key planning applications, has objected to Rochdale Council and Rochdale AFC’s plans for the hub at Bowlee Playing Fields. The plans are to create a training pitch for Rochdale AFC with a 3G pitch and grass pitch for Rochdale AFC Community Trust on one part of the council-owned site, with two 3G pitches and three grass pitches alongside cricket provision, a children’s playground and free parking for community use. As the plans affect the use of current playing fields, they have to meet one of Sport England’s five exception criteria in order for the body to support them. As well as changes to the existing playing field space and the exclusive use of certain areas by the club, Sport England raised concerns about the proposed Rochdale AFC pavilion’s community changing rooms. Its written response to the planning application states: “It is understood that the proposal would prejudice the use, or lead to the loss of use, of land being used as a playing field or has been used as a playing field in the last five years. An aerial view of the proposed Football and Community Wellbeing Hub at Bowlee Playing Fields in Middleton shows Rochdale AFC’s hub in the foreground and the community pitches in the background. Image: Rochdale AFC Community Trust “The proposal is on playing fields which currently support the delivery of both football and cricket at the site and there are a number of outstanding issues which need to be resolved in order it to comply with Exception 5 criteria.

candidates.source_summary: Middleton is changing, but the signs of its regeneration won’t be reduced to a ‘£6 oat milk latte’, according to Bev Craig.
candidates.source_body_excerpt:
Middleton is changing, but the signs of its regeneration won’t be reduced to  a ‘£6 oat milk latte’, according to Bev Craig.

At the Rochdale town’s arena last night (September 7), a different vision was laid out. Greater Manchester’s new mayor spoke of how Middletonians had felt forgotten for too long – and promised her backing for regeneration, with local opinions at its heart.

She took to the stage alongside actor and comedian Steve Coogan, CEO of Co-operatives UK Rose Marley and Rochdale council leader Neil Emmott to push forward the Middleton Mayoral Development Corporation (MDC).

This aims to bring Metrolink trams to Middleton; create new homes on brownfield plots; build high-quality business premises; and better public areas, roads and pathways. 

“It’s what people actually want to see,” Ms Craig told Middleton Arena. “It’s about doing things in a collective way. A £6 oat milk latte isn’t the sign of regeneration.”

While milk chat probably wasn’t what any of around 200 locals in attendance at the public event were expecting, it stood as a metaphor for what bosses are trying to do for the town.

A message of putting local needs first was the clear direction put forward. 

Bev Craig said: “Tonight is about showing how things can be done differently. It isn’t about development being done to people, it’s about people saying what they want the future of their town to be.

“This event is about listening, but showing we can back that up with action. Then get on and deliver for what the people of Middleton want to see.

“People are proud to be from Middleton. But when you look at the town centre, the banks have disappeared, the high street shops are closing down and they are wondering what their future is.

“In places like Middleton, the next 10 years can be a good 10 years. We are not accepting decline.

“Rochdale council has picked Middleton as the area they want their MDC for. My job as mayor is to spearhead that charge.

“People from Middleton are proud to be from Middleton. We wouldn’t have got someone like Steve Coogan if he didn’t believe in the place. That is what is really special about this.

“People care about here. Yes we’ve got star quality in Steve, but he’s here because he cares about Middleton. We all just want to see the best for a town that for too long, has felt like it’s been left behind.”

The future of the Mayoral Development Corporation was put forward in glitzy style, opening with a dance showcase from Tracing Steps.

Co-chairs Rose Marley and Alan Partridge creator Steve Coogan, who grew up in Alkrington, shared the findings of its ‘Our Town, Our Future’ project, which saw engagement with more than 2,000 residents. Locals, want less antisocial behaviour on the streets, shops coming back to their high street and visible investment in the town. 

Around a third of respondents said they would like to see Warwick Mill brought back into use. And that is was something the packed out auditorium got.

candidates.source_summary: A woman with a stoma bag is furious following string of missed bin collections. Jackie Allen has had various cancer treatment following bowel issues.
candidates.source_body_excerpt:
She says if her used stoma bags are left in the bin for too long, the smell is unbearable.

She is due to get a special bin to put her waste bags in, but has been putting them in the general waste bin in the meantime.

Jackie, from Spotland, is visually impaired and is supposed to get assistance from Rochdale council for collections.

Assisted collections involve bins being collected from people’s homes, rather than from the end of their drives. 

Jackie has reported numerous missed collections this year. The Churchill Street resident said: “I have to keep ringing the council to collect the bin. I use a stoma bag and they really smell.

“I said they should give me a free month from council tax because they just don’t collect them. 

“Every other week I have got to report it. It’s just not on. I’m partially sighted as well. It’s disgusting.

“It has been going on for months – the majority of 2026.”

Jackie is undergoing treatment for cancer and spends a lot of time travelling to and from hospital appointments. 

Having to organise bin collections is only adding to her stress, she said. 

“It makes me feel like they don’t care about me,” Jackie added. “It is stressing me out.

“I can’t live with a smell like that. I can’t go out into the garden because of the smell.”

Rochdale council officials recent visited Jackie. A spokesperson for the council said: “We’re sorry Ms Allen has experienced issues with her bin collections. We have since visited her and arranged for all her outstanding bins to be cleared. 

“Her property has also now been added to our watch list, so future collections can be monitored to make doubly sure that her bins are emptied when they should be.”

The UNISON union said the strike by more than 350 workers planned for Monday 14 September will not go ahead after discussions with the Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust (NCA). However, it said workers - including nurses, clinical support workers and housekeepers - will still walk out on Tuesday and Thursday next week unless there is "significant progress". candidates.source_body_excerpt: REGINA, Sask. — The rainfall that led to the outright collapse of an already-vulnerable sinkhole in northwest Regina over the Labour Day long weekend was part of what the city is calling a generational weather event. Speaking to reporters at city hall Tuesday afternoon, Regina’s water, waste and environment director Carolyn Kalim said parts of the city received up to 95 millimetres (about 3.8 inches) of rain over the course of Sunday and Monday. "We are looking at a one-in-50-year storm event in the northwest area of the city," Kalim said. One of the hardest-hit areas was Regina’s Rochdale neighbourhood, where a giant sinkhole developed at the intersection of Cunningham Drive and Stephens Bay, near the north entrance to Rochdale Park. “The city was aware of the sinkhole starting on Aug. 19 and we knew at that time that we needed to drain the stormwater pond that the pipe that failed discharges into,” said Kalim. “So that’s quite a process to get that done and we were going through that process to get it drained and working with our regulator, etcetera. “Obviously with the storm event we saw some deterioration of that sinkhole and so now we are kind of moving into a more emergent response for that and so we’re looking at the system to see what we can pump out into the stormwater system, what capacity is left there, to try and get that down as quickly as possible. “What that will do is it’ll allow us to access into the pipe system to actually do the inspection and see what is wrong with the pipe and from there we can determine the repair. So because we don’t know the repair, exactly what we need to do yet, we can’t give a specific timeline but it is a priority as soon as we can get that drained down.” Cunningham Drive resident Andrew Swanston confirmed in an interview with SaskToday that the distressed area had been a known concern prior to the weekend weather that caved it in.

Julie said the situation has worsened since walkers discovered the previously quiet spot during the pandemic. candidates.source_summary: Children with life-threatening allergies should be safer in schools following a new law to ensure staff know how to respond in an emergency
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Children with life-threatening allergies should be safer in schools following a new law to ensure staff know how to respond in an emergency. Nearly 700,000 children in England have a food allergy, with about two in every classroom affected, and it is an issue close to the heart of Rochdale MP and Minister for Early Education Paul Waugh. The changes introduced this month are known as Benedict’s Law, which requires every school in England to have a whole-school allergy policy, setting out how allergies are managed and how staff respond in an emergency. All staff must have allergy awareness training, including how to recognise a reaction and use an adrenaline auto-injector. Spare adrenaline auto-injectors must also be kept on site for emergencies, including for a child not previously known to have an allergy. Every pupil with a diagnosed allergy must have an individual healthcare or allergy action plan. Schools are one of the most common places outside the home where serious reactions happen, and many reactions occur in children not previously known to have an allergy. Regina received around 95 millilitres of rain — just under 4 inches — on Sunday and Monday combined, according to the city. Carolyn Kalim, director of water, waste and environment, said the high level of rain caused localized flooding, including multiple underpasses, ring road restrictions, and even caused the city to send out notices to its residents asking to conserve water on Monday, in order to alleviate pressure on the stormwater system. candidates.source_summary: The East Lancashire Railway has its first female steam locomotive driver after Steph Elwood successfully completed her driving assessments.
candidates.source_body_excerpt:
She progressed through the railway's steam department from cleaner to fireman before qualifying to drive steam locomotives.

Steph is now officially a Passed Fireman, allowing her to carry out both firing and driving turns on the heritage railway.

She said her interest in heritage railways began when she attended her first Santa Special at two months old.

Steph said: “I’m so pleased to be able to say that I’ve now successfully passed all my driving assessments to become the first female steam train driver at the East Lancashire Railway. It feels like such a huge achievement, and I still can’t quite believe that I’m now officially a Passed Fireman, allowing me to carry out both firing and driving turns.

“My love of heritage railways goes back to when I was just two months old, when I attended my first Santa Special. To think that, all these years later, I would be here achieving this is something I could never have imagined. From being a little girl fascinated by steam trains to now having the opportunity to drive one myself is a dream come true.

“I’m incredibly grateful to everyone who has supported, encouraged and helped me along the way. There have been challenges and a lot to learn, but every step of the journey has made reaching this moment even more rewarding.

“I hope my achievement will show other women that the railway really is a place for them. If my journey inspires even one woman to take that first step, get involved and discover what they can achieve, then I would be incredibly proud.”

Mike Kelly, chairman of the East Lancashire Railway, said: “I want to offer Steph my warmest congratulations on this outstanding achievement. Becoming a steam locomotive driver requires enormous commitment, determination, skill and passion, and Steph has demonstrated all of those qualities throughout her journey.

“What makes this achievement particularly special is that Steph has become the first female steam locomotive driver in the history of the East Lancashire Railway.

“She may not see herself as a pioneer or a role model, but she should take a moment to appreciate what she has achieved. By following the traditional route from cleaner through the steam crew ranks to the footplate, she has not only achieved her own ambition but has also helped to open the door for other women who may dream of becoming steam locomotive drivers.”

The East Lancashire Railway operates around 12 miles between Heywood, Bury, Ramsbottom and Rawtenstall.

It reopened to passengers in 1987 and is due to celebrate its 40th anniversary in 2027.

A small team of volunteers, along with friends and family, collected, sorted, washed, ironed and distributed the donated clothing throughout the summer.

Heywood Uniform Hub provides good-quality preloved uniform free of charge, with donated clothing reused rather than thrown away.

The Summer Uniform Hub has now finished and the organisation is preparing to move into a permanent base at Recovery Republic in Heywood.

The move will allow the group to continue providing uniform to families throughout the year.

Claire Yardley, director of Heywood Uniform Hub CIC, said the 6,443 items distributed during its first summer showed the level of community support for the project.

candidates.source_summary: Residents are being urged to check their electoral registration details to make sure they can vote on decisions that affect them.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Residents are being urged to check their electoral registration details to make sure they can vote on decisions that affect them. With local elections taking place in May, 2027, it’s an opportunity for residents to make sure they can take part. The annual canvass allows Rochdale Borough Council to keep the electoral register up to date, to identify who risks losing their voice at elections, and encourage them to register before it’s too late. Edward McCreadie, elections manager at Rochdale Borough Council, said: “Over the summer we’ve sent emails to residents in over 40,000 properties asking them to check their details and update if necessary and this week follow up letters were sent, so do keep an eye out. “The annual canvass is our way of making sure that the information on the electoral register for every address is accurate and up to date. “To make sure you don’t lose your say at upcoming elections, simply follow the instructions sent to you.
